<description>
{
 "summary": "Adds early validation checks during transaction and block deserialization to fail fast on malformed data. Transactions with impossible input or output counts are rejected globally, while P2P deserialization rejects transactions with zero inputs or outputs and aborts if total weight exceeds the 4M block limit. To track weight during deserialization without breaking streaming abstractions, it introduces caller-owned state tracking into the serialization framework.",
 "problem": "Nodes currently fully deserialize invalid P2P messages before validation rejects them, enabling worst-case memory and CPU consumption. A peer can send a 4 MB block message containing up to 16M weight, up to 400,000 empty transactions that each allocate a CTransaction object, or transactions with inflated input/output counts that trigger repeated 5 MB vector reallocations.",
 "evidence": [
  "Commit 9de186b527 calculates that roughly 400,000 10-byte zero-input/zero-output transactions can fit in a single 4 MB block message, each triggering separate CTransaction allocations before validation rejects them.",
  "Commit aaea704057 notes that current P2P message limits allow blocks of up to 4 MB (representing up to 16M weight) to be completely deserialized before validation rejection.",
  "Commit 039f5ce69d notes that bounding input and output counts to block limits caps initial vector allocations to 2.7 MB and 5.3 MB respectively, avoiding sequential 5 MB reallocation steps."
 ],

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
